fields: IAM's name
islands set
In the field's terms
Constitutively unmethylated CpG island set (CpG islands unmethylated in every healthy cell type)
Definition
The set of 66,986 CpG island sites (IAM-Atlas v2.1 territory sets; source iam_a.sites.islands) that every healthy type keeps unmarked.
What it does

It defines the sites the islands meter reads. In a healthy sample, methylated calls at these sites are the library's own false calls (incomplete conversion, sequencing error), which correct the other readings; a rise above that level is real methylation gain at islands.
Why the instrument needs it

Because incomplete conversion and sequencing error produce some false methylated calls even in a healthy sample, the instrument needs a baseline of sites that should always read unmarked so it can tell the library's own noise apart from a genuine gain.
How it is obtained or computed
Taken from iam_a.sites.islands (IAM-Atlas v2.1 territory sets), basis measured. The meter reads the sample's own molecules at these sites (source_kind: read from the sample's own molecules).
Where it is read
66,986 island sites drawn from the IAM-Atlas v2.1 territory sets.
Where IAM's Law enters
Not part of IAM's Law: the packet marks this as not the law itself, but a measured input the law uses.

not part of IAM's Law

Not a reading with its own healthy band: it is a fixed set of 66,986 island sites that every healthy type keeps unmarked (iam_a.sites.islands, basis measured).

the gain-side molecule rule (QUAL_MAX_METH)
In the field's terms
Per-read methylation cutoff for counting a molecule as unmethylated (maximum methylated share allowed on one read)
Definition
A rule, value QUAL_MAX_METH 0.2, that marks a molecule as 'held unmarked' (plain: 'a molecule held unmarked') for the purposes of the islands meter's dust correction.
What it does
Each molecule is judged against QUAL_MAX_METH 0.2 to decide whether it counts as a molecule held unmarked (plain: 'a molecule held unmarked'). It is a rule inside the islands meter (instrument 7).
Why the instrument needs it

The instrument needs this rule to do the dust correction: it reads methylated calls at CpG islands that every healthy type in the atlas keeps unmethylated, and in a healthy sample these are the library's own false calls (incomplete conversion, sequencing error), which correct the other readings; a rise above that level is read as real methylation gain at islands.

Obtained as a rule (basis: rule) from stage_q2_selfref.QUAL_MAX_METH, read from the sample's own molecules (source_kind), value QUAL_MAX_METH 0.2; it is in_chain: yes.
Where it is read
Applied to calls at CpG islands that every healthy type in the atlas keeps unmethylated, per the instrument's job; no further genomic coordinate is given for this rule itself.

fields: IAM's name
conversion spike-in
In the field's terms
Conversion-efficiency spike-in control (a control DNA added to the library to measure incomplete conversion directly)
Definition

An optional input that would measure each library's own conversion-failure rate directly; in every library in the atlas this input is absent, so conv_fail reads null (value: "none in atlas libraries (conv_fail null)").
What it does

When a library carries one, it is a second meter of the library's own conversion failure, read from the sample's own molecules (source iam_a.count.conv_fail; card key conv). No atlas library carries one (conv_fail null), so for those libraries the islands meter (instrument 7) is the only reading of the false-mark rate.
Why the instrument needs it

The islands meter (instrument 7) reads each library's own false methylation calls (incomplete conversion, sequencing error), which correct the other readings. A conversion spike-in, when the library has one, is a second meter for that rate.
How it is obtained or computed

Obtained, when present, by measurement from the sample's own molecules (source_kind: read from the sample's own molecules; source: iam_a.count.conv_fail; basis: measured when present). No formula is given in the record. In the atlas libraries this step yields nothing, since conv_fail is null.
Where it is read
not genome-located

Islands held error and gain
In the field's terms
Methylation gain and held (maintenance) error at CpG islands every healthy cell keeps unmethylated; in a healthy sample the gain is the library's false-methylation rate
Definition
The held error and gain error measured at CpG islands — the territory every healthy cell type always keeps unmarked.
What it does

It performs the dust correction: it reads methylated calls at CpG islands that every healthy type in the atlas keeps unmethylated, giving each library its own false-mark rate; a rise above that level is read as real methylation gain at islands.
Why the instrument needs it

The chain needs to know a library's own false-call rate at a site that should never be marked, so that methylation signal seen elsewhere can be corrected against that library's background rather than mistaken for it.
How it is obtained or computed

It reads methylated calls at CpG islands that every healthy type in the atlas keeps unmethylated. In a healthy sample these calls are the library's own false calls (incomplete conversion, sequencing error), which correct the other readings; a rise above that level is real methylation gain at islands. It is computed by the chain from the sample's molecules and its references, and in this run the test state came back OK.
Where it is read

At the islands territory (stage_metaa_atlas.territory_sets, IAM-Atlas v2.1) — each library's own meter, the islands every healthy cell type keeps unmarked — across 66986 probes, read at path iam_a.sites.islands.
Where IAM's Law enters
Not part of IAM's Law: law_part 'not the law: instrument or meter', long-form section 'not part of IAM's Law'. It is a measured meter reading of each library's own false-mark rate.

record.reads_from: molecules (each read followed CpG by CpG; needs a molecule file)

fields: How it works

Reads methylated calls on mostly unmethylated molecules (at most 20 % methylated) at 66,986 CpG-island sites that every healthy type in the atlas keeps unmarked. In a healthy sample those calls are the library's own false marks (incomplete bisulfite conversion plus sequencing error): the meter, which corrects the other readings. A rise above it is real methylation gain at islands.
Why

Every library has its own false-mark rate; measuring it inside the sample, where the true answer is known to be unmarked, removes the laboratory part without healthy samples from the same run (the 2026-11-07 reference rule).
Physics
Not a step of IAM's Law: the instrument's own calibration. It sets the zero that the gain-side readings and the law's floor are read above.
Where the data comes from

The sample's molecules; the island set (IAM-Atlas v2.1 territory sets, 66,986 sites); a conversion spike-in when present (none in the atlas libraries, so conv_fail reads null and the meter is the island gain itself).
The numbers

Test library GSM5652214: island gain 0.00432 (741 methylated calls on mostly unmethylated molecules over 171,550 chances at the always-unmarked islands; iam_a.sites.islands.gain_err), against the whole-sample gain 0.0141 (iam_a.count.gain_err, 4,731,319 chances); healthy islands expectation about 0.004 (T1). Relay test: planted island gain moved the meter 0.0043 -> 0.052 and territory islands x9.96, IAM-A x1.002 (independent).
Method and standard
Counted rate at sites known to be unmarked (a dark frame); the healthy bar by the 2026-11-07 rule from held-out libraries (owed).
Known-answer test
Relay test (2026-11-20): planted island gain moved the meter 0.0043 -> 0.052 and the island territories, not IAM-A (met). Cross-talk: clock sites that are islands rose 0.0123 -> 0.0140.
Limits

(1) No measured healthy bar yet. (2) Without a spike-in, conversion failure and sequencing error are not separated (the meter names which was used). (3) True island gain in a sample and a bad library look alike in one reading; a library's other readings and its ends separate them.
Where the result goes
bundle iam_a.count (gain_err, gain_opp, meter, conv_fail, tc_err); used as the zero for island gain, the territories and the clock; report.
Code
stage_q2_selfref counter (gain side, QUAL_MAX_METH 0.2); meter state in run_sample.py
How to rebuild it
1. Pick island sites every healthy atlas type keeps unmarked. 2. On molecules at most 20 % methylated there, count methylated calls over chances. 3. Check slope against the spike-in where present.
History
Dated entries in the development log (METHYLPHYS_DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md) and the instrument's development record.
records.name: Islands meter: each library's own false-mark rate, read where no healthy cell marks
questions: Why not use a spike-in for conversion?
Most public libraries have none; the islands every healthy type keeps unmarked are a spike-in already inside every sample.
register T1 (53 libraries)
How is real island gain told from a bad library?
In one reading they look alike; a library's ends, its other readings and its depth separate them, and the planted test shows the meter moves only for island gain.
relay test
What exactly does this instrument measure?

It looks at methylated calls at 66,986 CpG-island sites that every healthy cell type in the reference atlas keeps unmethylated. In a healthy sample, any methylated call there isn't real biology — it's the library's own false call from incomplete bisulfite conversion or sequencing error, and that rate is used to correct the other readings.
field_how; rule description
Why not just use a synthetic spike-in to measure conversion efficiency instead?

Most public libraries don't include a spike-in control at all. The always-unmethylated islands act as a spike-in that's already present in every sample, so this method doesn't depend on labs having added one.
existing_qa, first question; rule 'why' field
Can this tell incomplete bisulfite conversion apart from sequencing error?

Not yet recorded: the packet states that without an added spike-in control, conversion failure and sequencing error can't be separated — the correction only reports which type of error correction was applied, not what fraction came from each source.
rule limits, point 2; outputs field 'Conversion failure'
How do you distinguish a true rise in island methylation from a poorly performing library?

One reading alone cannot tell them apart; the library's other readings, depth and read-end quality are read beside it. Planted incomplete conversion (1% of unmethylated calls) raised this meter by 0.00973 against 0.0099 predicted while the biology readings stayed within 0.3%, and the same plant raised whole-sample Met-A by 4.3%, so this meter is what separates a laboratory effect from a biological one.
planted answer 2026-11-22 (incomplete conversion)
What's the expected baseline reading in a healthy sample?

In a healthy sample, the expected island gain is about 0.004, which corresponds to the library's own false-call rate. This figure was established by direct measurement rather than estimated or assumed.
outputs field 'Islands held error and gain', healthy_how
Is there a healthy range across the atlas libraries, beyond correcting each library against itself?
Not yet: it is being built now from the molecule pass over the atlas's healthy libraries (one observed normal operating range, Student's t), and checked on libraries never used to build it.
plan step 11
Do any of the atlas libraries have a conversion spike-in that could sharpen this correction?

No. The packet states that none of the atlas libraries carry a conversion spike-in, so there is no secondary check available to separate conversion failure from sequencing error in any of these samples — this is recorded as a known gap, not estimated around.
inputs field 'conversion spike-in', limits
